power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p=<0.001", Text = "AML disease stage at HCT was the strongest predictor of OS with mortality risk increasing progressively from 1 st complete remission (CR1, reference) to active disease (hazard ratio, HR=1.1, p=0.01 for CR2; and 1.45, p=0.002 for CR3+; and 1.93, p=<0.001 for active disease)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.76", "p = 0.76"), Sentence = c("In donors, CHIP-PGS did not differ by age (p=0.76) but was modestly lower in unrelated vs. related donors (-0.06 standard deviation [SD]; p=0.002).", "Using cohort-wide standardized PGS, no statistically significant differences in PGS distribution were noted between younger and older donors (<35 vs ≥35 years: adjusted difference -0.004 SD, p = 0.76) (Figure 3C)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Background: Genomic studies in hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) are limited by sample sizes and targeted approaches.

Methods: The Genomic Studies in Blood and Marrow Transplantation (GS-BMT) project is a collaboration between the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the CIBMTR® designed to investigate recipient and donor determinants of HCT outcomes.
We are generating genome-wide SNP-array genotyping for all samples, and sequencing and methylation profiling for selected subsets.

We report study design and cohort characteristics and present two proof-of-concept analyses: comparison of conventional and machine learning prediction of overall survival after HCT in 9,262 patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and assessment of inherited susceptibility to clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) among 19,750 HCT donors using polygenic scores (PGS).
Results: GS-BMT includes 30,718 donor-recipient pairs who received allogeneic HCT in the United States between 2000 and 2019.

In AML, clinical variables alone provided modest prediction for post-transplant survival, with similar performance for Cox proportional hazards, random survival forest, and deep neural network survival models (C-index=0.63, 0.62, and 0.62, respectively).
In donors, CHIP-PGS did not differ by age (p=0.76) but was modestly lower in unrelated vs. related donors (-0.06 standard deviation [SD]; p=0.002).

In an illustrative analysis assuming risk of event increases by 50% or 80% per PGS-SD, the top 5.2% and 12.3% of the donors, respectively, would have at least twice the risk of a donor with the average PGS.

Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) is a well-recognized curative therapy for several life-threatening hematologic diseases, with >8,000 recipients annually in the United States. 1 Acute leukemias, myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), and myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) combined account for approximately two-thirds of the cases. 1, 2 HCT methods have advanced over the last two decades leading to significant survival improvements (3-year probability of overall survival= 45.3% in 2002-2006 versus 62.1% in 2017-2022). 3 Some of the recent advances include the introduction of post-transplant cyclophosphamide for graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) prophylaxis that allowed for expanding donor selection to haplo-identical related and human leukocyte antigen (HLA) mismatched unrelated donors, the development of new immunomodulatory agents to treat severe chronic GvHD, and the development of new conditioning regimens that decreased organ toxicity and expanded transplant eligibility to older patients. 4, 5, 6 The significant role of genomics in HCT was recognized from its inception with a focus on immunogenetics particularly for HLA genes.

text.text: The Genomic Studies in Blood and Marrow Transplantation (GS-BMT) project is a collaboration between the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the CIBMTR® (Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research), representing the largest HCT genomic project to-date.
GS-BMT is designed to allow for the inclusion of both malignant and non-malignant diseases, all ages and ethnic groups, and different treatment regimens.
The project includes SNP-array genotyping for all recipient-donor pairs as well as sequencing and methylation array for selected cohort subsets.

This report describes the GS-BMT methodology and population characteristics, evaluates different predictive tools of HCT survival in the GS-BMT AML cohort using clinical information and presents an example of the effective use of these genomic data in donor selection focusing on susceptibility to clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP).

Current donor selection practices prioritize young donors (typically <30 years of age), which reduces the likelihood of prevalent CHIP, but likely does not control for its underlying genetic predisposition.

The study aims to 1) identify recipient and donor germline genetic variation and somatic alterations associated with HCT outcomes; 2) develop individualized risk calculators for post-HCT overall and event-free survival by incorporating key genomic and clinical factors; 3) characterize the germline genetic etiology of selected hematological malignancies (both common and rare risk variants); and 4) build and maintain a robust genomic data resource available for use by the HCT scientific community.
The study primary end points are all-cause and cause-specific mortality, and disease relapse.

Secondary end points include: 1) GvHD-free, relapse-free survival, defined as survival without grade III-IV acute GvHD, chronic GvHD requiring systemic therapy, or relapse; and 2) risk of subsequent malignancies

HCT recipients were eligible to be included in the study if they: 1) received HCT at a U.S. center between 2000-2019; and 2) had available clinical data and pre-HCT blood sample for both recipient and corresponding donor.
The study excluded cord transplants, diseases for which allogeneic HCT is not a standard of care (e.g., lymphoma), and rare HCT indications (<300 cases during the study period).

text.text: DNA was extracted from frozen whole blood or peripheral mononuclear cells using an automated high-throughput bead-based method (ThermoFisher; KingFisher).

Samples were genotyped on the customized Illumina Infinium Global Screening Array version 3.0 (GSA-V3), which interrogates approximately 743,000 markers with enrichment for low-frequency variants and multi-ethnic coverage.
Genotypes were called using the standard Illumina array-analysis workflow with a study-specific cluster file and aligned to genome build GRCh38.

Genotyping quality control (QC) included sample-and variant-level quality filters, sample identity verification (contamination, sex, technical replicates), and population structure characterization (ancestry inference, relatedness, genetic principal components [PCs]).
Imputation was carried out against the TOPMed r3 reference panel.
Full details of genotyping, imputation, and QC metrics are provided in the Supplemental Methods.

text.text: GS-BMT, the largest genomic investigation in HCT to date, holds great promise in refining donor selection, defining HCT outcomes, and advancing precision medicine for this population.

In this manuscript, we showed that clinical factors alone have modest ability to predict survival after HCT, and that the use of different machine-learning algorithms was not superior to conventional time-to-event analysis.
We also characterized inherited susceptibility to CHIP among donors, which was similar in younger and older donors, and illustrated how this could translate into differences in outcome risk.
These findings highlight the importance of integrating genomic data with clinical information to improve risk prediction, optimize donor selection, and advance precision HCT practices.
Advances in machine learning (ML) algorithms enable the handling of large high dimensional clinical and multi-omic data to guide precision medicine approaches.

text.text: Several recent studies highlighted the importance of germline genetic testing before HCT to guide patient risk stratification.

Examples include testing for rare pathogenic germline variants in inherited bone marrow failure genes for patients with severe aplastic anemia or MDS, or DNA repair genes before radiation-based conditioning regimens. [23] [24] [25] However, genetic screening of HCT donors remains focused on HLA compatibility and targeted testing based on the recipient's medical history with some assessment of recipient post-HCT variants, usually CHIP, suspected to be of donor origin. 26 Previous studies showed that the presence of CHIP variants in donors increased the risk of chronic GvHD and possibly donor-derived leukemia in HCT recipients. 27, 28 In our proof-of-concept analysis characterizing CHIP predisposition in HCT donors using polygenic genetic scores (PGS), we showed no differences in CHIP PGS by age consistent with their germline nature.

Genomic and clinical data from the GS-BMT will enable further investigation of whether donor inherited susceptibility to CHIP is associated with recipient outcomes, or age-related complications after HCT.

This is particularly important in light of prior evidence of accelerated biological aging in HCT recipients. 32, 33 In conclusion, GS-BMT is a large registry-based multi-center study designed to establish the foundation for HCT genomics, where donor selection can be guided by key genomic markers, and patient treatment regimens can be personalized to their genetic background.
